items.title: Life choices are money choices (II)

items.content_html:
PART ONE — THE DECISION

 
S$180. That was the fare, Changi to Tân Sơn Nhất and back. I paid it twenty-six times in six months.
 
Monday to Friday I ran a regional portfolio for a U.S. technology group — business laptops and IT solutions into large corporates across Asia-Pacific. Saturday morning I was in a hospital corridor in Saigon. Sunday night I was back at Changi, ironing a shirt for Monday. I did not have a weekend for half a year. I didn't notice, because there was nothing else to notice.
 
The flights came to S$4,680. I know that number because I have always known my numbers. What I didn't know until it was over was the other one: a hundred thousand US dollars. Everything I had saved in France. Everything I had saved in Singapore. The treatment. Roughly two years of my entire Singapore net income. About fifty-seven times what the average Vietnamese earned in a year in 2012.
 
In health economics there is a term for this — catastrophic health expenditure. It is not a metaphor. It is a threshold, and I was multiple past it. In Vietnam that year the insurer of last resort was not a policy. It was your family's own balance sheet. Out-of-pocket spending sat near 40% of total health expenditure. Coverage has widened a great deal since. But in that corridor, in that year, the policy was me.
 
Mom died. Then I moved home.
 
Everyone assumes the first caused the second. It didn't. I had already decided to return, and for a reason that has nothing to do with grief.
 
That year I sat in a bidding room quoting a Japanese retail conglomerate, group-wide, and a Vietnamese telecom group that was climbing. The Vietnamese order came in at three times the Japanese one — laptops, licensed software, accessories, warranty. In the slowest growth year this country had seen since 1999, a domestic group was building a salaried workforce at three times the scale of a Japanese blue chip.
 
Licensed software meant they were paying real money to formalize. A warranty package meant someone in that building was costing total ownership — which meant a finance function with actual authority. Salaried headcount is the leading indicator of the modern-trade basket, with a lag of a couple of years. I was reading the Vietnamese consumer of 2015 in a 2012 procurement document. No dashboard in Singapore was going to tell me that for two more years.
 
I remember thinking: this is the place to be. Not eventually. Now.
 
Then three multinationals bid for me at once, and I understood something else — that whatever the market thought of Vietnam, it did not think there were many of me. I had six headhunters approaching at the Finance Manager and Deputy Director level. Three offers closed. Four conversations were still open when I signed. In Singapore that same year I was a Senior Financial Analyst, and my own plan had me reaching, potentially, Manager in 2016. Vietnam offered me the grade four years early. Not because I was better there. Because there were fewer of me.
 
People ask why I took the lowest offer of the three. I didn't. I took the one with the most in it.
 
The three offers were not three salaries. They were three bets with different shapes.
 
The U.S. semiconductor group paid the most and told me the least about this country. A chip assembly plant is a cost centre inside an export bubble — you report variance and transfer-pricing and learn almost nothing about what a Vietnamese family does with its first pay rise. The U.S. consumer-goods giant paid well and handed me somebody else's playbook. The French retail distribution group paid the least and asked me to build the function from nothing — financial control from purchase centre to site, retail margin and rental roll — in a market that did not yet have the job title.
 
It was the steepest learning curve available, the fastest way to read a middle class being born in front of us, and the one position where whatever I built would have my name on it.
 
I did not take a pay cut. I bought the cheapest entry into the highest-upside position in the market. That is not generosity to Vietnam. That is an investment.
 
It was assessed the way I would assess any capital deployment. Downside: I had no savings, so a failure would hurt. Upside: large and skewed — a built function, a name, a career that compounds instead of one that rents. And the alternative's risk was the one nobody prices: a strong base on a commoditized path in a market where I was abundant. That risk arrives as a four per cent review and an unchanged title, and looks like safety for fourteen years. I took the sharp risk over the dull one. Sharp risks you can see and survive. Dull ones you cannot.
 
But the investment only worked because the alternative was structurally closed.
 
The woman I wanted to marry looked for work in Singapore. She did not find any. Not because she was not capable, but because she needed an Employment Pass she could not get, in a market the authorities had just tightened. As my girlfriend she had no dependant route. Staying meant one salary. And one salary in Singapore, for the life we wanted, did not close.
 
In Saigon she needed no pass. Her savings went into the down payment alongside mine — five hundred million đồng, two people, one flat, ninety square metres, a pool, a riverside park.
 
I did not come home for the salary. I came home because Singapore could not hold the life I was trying to build, and Vietnam could hold it on one income.
 
Fourteen years later I am a CFO. The initial scarcity premium — twenty-four per cent, then twenty-two, then twenty, tapering down to fifteen — was the market manufacturing people like me. The curve did not flatten because I did not sit on that advantage. I moved from retail into five further industries, each time stepping into a mandate the local market could not yet fill, each time resetting the scarcity clock before the previous premium finished eroding. Scarcity is not something you own. It is something you have to keep earning.
 
I might have been wrong. I bought the flat in 2015, before the property run, and I will not pretend that timing was entirely skill. The consumer-goods giant at thirty-five million was probably the better line on my CV for five years. Plenty who came home in 2012 with better papers got stuck. I am a survivor of this trade describing it, not a proof of it.
 
Mom never saw the flat. That is the one line I cannot make balance.
 

PART TWO — THE AUDIT TRAIL

What follows is the financial model underlying the 2012 decision, executed January 2013 and lived through to 2026. Every cell is sourced. Nothing is projected from memory.

1. The payroll reconstruction (2012/2013)

The "21% pay cut" narrative collapses under the actual tax and social-insurance law of the period. All offers were gross monthly. Under the law as it stood — employee social contributions at 9.5%, applied against the statutory minimum-wage ceilings, personal deduction at VND 4m/month before the July 2013 revision — the net picture was:
Offer
Gross/mo
Social
PIT
Net/mo
U.S. semiconductor group (sign-on amortised)
30.0m + bonus
2.085m
4.133m
28.78m
U.S. consumer-goods giant
35.0m
2.135m
4.123m
28.74m
French retail distribution group
27.5m
2.060m
2.638m
22.80m
The semiconductor group's two-month sign-on put it effectively on par with the consumer-goods giant in Year 1. From Year 2 it fell to 24.78m — under two million above the retail group. The real net gap I accepted against the consumer-goods offer was roughly 6m a month.

2. Scarcity decay versus the realised CAGR

This is the most important finding in the model — and the one that separates an audit from a victory lap.
 
The taper (scarcity decay). The retail group's offer implied an initial raise trajectory of ~24%, decaying year by year to ~15%. That decay is the sound of the market manufacturing substitutes for the 2012 returnee profile.
 
The realised CAGR. From VND 27.5m in February 2013 to VND 171m in 2026 is a multiple of 6.22x — a 15.1% compound annual rate. This is not a single-firm ladder. It is the market repricing my capability across a French retail network and then five further firms in five further industries.
 
The inference. A decaying initial premium cannot produce a sustained 15% compound over thirteen years inside one role. The realised CAGR proves the initial advantage was replaced by successive scarcity positions — each move into a sector the local market could not yet supply leadership for, resetting the scarcity clock before the previous premium finished eroding. Scarcity here is not inherited. It is re-earned at every border crossed.

3. The housing ledger — the structural wall

This is where the Singapore counterfactual mathematically fails for a mono-income household.
 
Vietnam (actual). Purchased a 90 sqm riverside condominium in 2015 for VND 1.5 billion. VND 500m joint down payment; VND 1b mortgage on a ten-year tenor; settled early in 2020 through aggressive saving, with ~VND 400m total interest paid over sixty months. Total cash deployed: VND 1.9 billion.Current market value: VND 3.5 billion. Imputed market rent VND 15m/month — a gross yield of 5.14%— debt-free.
 
Singapore (counterfactual). To replicate a 90 sqm, two-bedroom private condominium with full facilities requires an asset of roughly S$1.8m–2.0m. As a foreign national on an Employment Pass, the Additional Buyer's Stamp Duty applies. Introduced at 10% for foreigners in December 2011, it rose to 15% in January 2013, 20% in 2018, 30% in 2021, and 60% in April 2023. At the current rate, the stamp duty alone on a S$1.9m property is ~S$1.14 million — a pure dead-weight loss paid before a single brick is owned. Even at the 2013 rate of 15%, the dead-weight loss was ~S$285,000 — prohibitive for a mono-income household struggling to close a monthly basket. The Singapore path rents forever. The Vietnam path converts cash into a yielding, debt-free asset.

4. The family basket multiple (2026 endpoint)

We do not compare salaries at nominal FX. We compare net income against the cost of an equivalent comfortable family life — spouse, one secondary-school child.
 
Vietnam (actual, 2026). Gross VND 171m/month plus a 2.5-month average bonus gives ~VND 2,479m annual gross. Net monthly income, averaged with current dependent deductions: ~VND 147.6m. The all-in household basket is VND 60m ongoing plus ~VND 11m of averaged lumpy costs — gifts to both families, hiếu hỉ, overseas travel, home improvements — totalling VND 71m. Add VND 15m imputed rent on the owned flat for a full economic cost of VND 86m.
Basket multiple: 147.6 ÷ 86 = 1.72x. Net income buys 1.7 times the full economic family standard.
 
Singapore (market-anchored counterfactual, 2026). Associate Director, S$15,000 base plus a two-month bonus = S$210,000 annual gross. Net after resident tax: ~S$15,595. Equivalent family basket — S$5,000 rent for the comparable condominium, S$3,000 secondary school, S$7,000 food, transport, household, insurance, travel — totalling S$15,000.
Basket multiple: 15,595 ÷ 15,000 = 1.04x. On one income at the equivalent standard, the Associate Director barely covers the basket. No capital left to buy the home. No buffer for a shock.
 
(A cheaper Singapore life exists — public housing, local school, a basket near S$10,500 — but that is a different life, not a cheaper version of the same one. We hold the standard constant. A stalled-path branch, Senior Financial Analyst at 4% throughout with no promotion, ends at ~S$8,658/month in 2026.)

5. The reconciliation and the relational ledger

Running a smooth 15% interpolation against a 10m→60m living-cost curve yields a modelled cumulative cash surplus of roughly VND 5.6 billion. The reported cash position in 2026 is ~US$150,000 (≈ VND 3.9 billion).
 
The ~VND 1.7 billion gap is not an error. It is the relational ledger — roughly VND 11m a month over thirteen years deployed into the Vietnamese family structure: supporting parents, wedding envelopes, funeral envelopes, the unquantifiable cost of holding a family network together. This is the Vietnamese household's actual insurance premium. It does not appear in any international cost-of-living table, but it is the most durable line item on the balance sheet.
 

6. Sources & methodology

  • Vietnam macro & stabilization: GSO GDP and CPI series, 2011–2012; State Bank of Vietnam Resolution 11/NQ-CP (February 2011) on macro stabilization and inflation control.
  • Tax & social insurance: Vietnam Personal Income Tax Law 04/2007/QH12 and Law 22/2012/QH13 (personal deduction VND 4m); Social Insurance Law 58/2014/QH13; minimum-wage decrees defining contribution ceilings by year. Singapore IRAS resident individual tax rates.
  • Property & stamp duty: Singapore IRAS ABSD rate trajectory, December 2011 to April 2023; URA rental transactions for ~900–1,000 sqft private condominiums; HCMC market transactions for 90 sqm riverside units.
  • Labour market: Singapore Ministry of Manpower Employment Pass qualifying-salary revisions, 2011–2012; Robert Walters / Michael Page / Hays Singapore salary guides, 2016 / 2020 / 2026, for Finance Manager / Senior Manager / Associate Director benchmarking.
  • Health economics: World Bank / WHO Global Health Expenditure Database, Vietnam out-of-pocket share of current health expenditure, 2012 series.
 
 
This is Post 2 of the CestViet series "Life choices are money choices." Post 3 will document the execution — the five further industries between 2013 and 2026, the lessons that fueled the path to CFO, and the structural particularities that make Vietnam reward operational leadership differently from other markets.

items.title: Life choices are money choices (I)
items.summary:
Everyone pitied my S$5,000 "local contract." Nobody ran the math.
 
Picture this: early 2010, France. You're graduating top of your class with a master's in finance and banking. Big-name banks are already sliding offers across the table.
 
The catch: a six-month countdown for a work permit — and nobody can promise you'll get it.
 
You've spent seven years building a life here from zero. The language. The friends. The belonging.
 
Now, the machine you were up against. None of it was personal — and that was the problem.
 
The market. Wall Street broke in 2008; French hiring broke in 2009. Unemployment jumped from 7.4% to 9.1% in a year. For under-25s: roughly one in four. And of the young people who did have jobs, about half were on temporary contracts. Translation: companies weren't hiring people. They were renting them.
 
The clock. The 2006 immigration law — its philosophy was literally called immigration choisie, "selective immigration" — gave non-EU master's graduates exactly one concession: six months to find a qualifying job. Non-renewable. A countdown, not a safety net. Bachelor's grads didn't even get the countdown.
 
The fine print. The job had to match your degree and pay at least 1.5× the minimum wage — about €2,000 gross a month in 2010. Miss either box, and your employer had to prove no one already on the French labor market could do your job. Try proving a labor shortage in a year when a quarter of your generation was jobless.
 
The mood. This was the era of a Ministry of Immigration, Integration and National Identity, annual deportation targets, and a state-sponsored "Great Debate on National Identity." No one had to ban you. The message lived in the paperwork: months-long queues, discretion at every counter, and employers who needed someone who could start Monday.
On paper, a top-of-class master's grad with bank offers was exactly the immigrant this system claimed to want. On paper.
 
So what do you do? Follow your heart and bet a decade of your life on a maybe? Or follow your head, pack up, and go somewhere that actually wants you?
 
Here's what nobody tells you — and school never teaches: this was never just a heart-vs-head decision. It was a long-term money question in disguise.
Plot twist: that wasn't a hypothetical. That was me — a Vietnamese grad, seven years into a French life built from zero. And I left.
 
One-way ticket to Singapore. A "local contract" with regional scope at a U.S. tech giant: S$5,000 a month. No expat housing. No relocation package. Seven years of belonging, packed into checked luggage. People back in France gave me that polite, tilted-head sympathy.
 
Everyone pitied the local contract. Nobody ran the math.
Here it is on a napkin. Rough numbers — but they're my numbers.
 
The lottery ticket vs. the sure thing. A French bank offer paid about €40,000 a year — if a prefecture let me take it. Six months of waiting first: no salary, about €1,000 a month of Paris rent and food, and a clerk with discretion at the end of it. A job offer you might not be allowed to accept isn't an offer. It's a lottery ticket with a rent bill. Singapore? A salary comfortably above the Employment Pass bar, paperwork measured in days, and a start date.
 
The haircut. In France, roughly 30 cents of every euro I earned vanished before I paid rent — social charges, then income tax. In Singapore, about 5. Same person, same work, radically different haircut. And yes — France's 30% bought a pension and healthcare. Singapore's 5% meant the safety net was mine to build. Fine. I'd rather build it myself with the other 25 cents. Singapore also didn't tax investment gains. France did.
 
Do the six-month math: start in Singapore, save roughly €9,000 after rent and food. Wait in Paris, burn roughly €6,000. That coin flip cost about €15,000 — win or lose. And I was saving in a currency that gained about 14% against the euro that year alone.
 
The refund policy. Here's the part nobody tells you. The Singapore move was reversible: if it failed, I'd still have the French master's, a Fortune 500 line on my CV, and savings in a hard currency. The Paris wait was the irreversible one. The permit was non-renewable. So is your time.
 
The price tag. In France, I was one of thousands of identical graduates with a visa problem. You don't set your price in a market oversupplied with you. In Singapore, a finance grad with Vietnamese and French, covering APAC for an American tech company, was a scarcity. Your market value isn't a personality trait. It's a location.
 
And the scariest line item wasn't financial. My English was weak. Regional calls, in my third language, with executives who didn't slow down for anyone. Seven years of classrooms hadn't done what twelve months of those calls did. Vietnamese, French, English — three languages, three markets. And Saigon was suddenly a two-hour flight away instead of twelve.
 
The verdict. France's unemployment didn't peak in 2010. It kept climbing until 2015, to around 10%. I didn't abandon the ship at the worst moment. I left five years before it stopped sinking.
 
The lesson. You're not choosing between Paris and Singapore. But you're choosing something: the "safe" job in a shrinking industry. The city that eats half your salary. The path you're staying on because of the years already spent.
 
Run the napkin math. Not because money is everything — because money is the part everyone politely refuses to count.
 
Every life-changing decision is a long-term money decision. And the worst markets hide the best entry prices.
 
Resilience isn't proving you can survive a bad market. It's refusing to donate your best years to one. Grit without math is just expensive stubbornness.
Numbers: INSEE, IRAS, MOM, MAS — rounded, 2008–2015. The napkin math is mine. Rules: CESEDA as in force in 2009–2010; they've changed since. The rest: public record, and a life lived through it.

Still here? This part is the audit trail — for the finance crowd.

The CFO's cut of a personal decision: France vs. Singapore, 2010

Prestige is not a cash flow. I reduced the decision to CFO math: execution risk, tax wedge, living costs, savings rate, currency, and reversibility. What follows is probability-weighted, after-tax, and period-correct (2009–2011). Assumptions are labeled; they are mine, not statistics.

1. Assumptions

Input
Value
Status
Paris offer
€40,000 gross/yr
My offer; within the €36–42k range for top finance grads
Singapore contract
S$60,000 gross/yr (S$5,000/mo)

Conservative

2. Execution risk: a conditional offer is not an asset

France. Under CESEDA art. L.311-11 (2006 framework), a master's graduate with a job related to the degree paying ≥1.5× SMIC was exempt from the labor market test (opposabilité de la situation de l'emploi). At ~€2,006/month gross (SMIC €8.82/h × 151.67h × 1.5, July 2009), the €40k offer cleared it. The binding constraints were not the test. They were: a six-month, non-renewable job-search permit; prefecture processing measured in months; employer start-date intolerance; and a discretionary rejection tail.
 
Singapore. S$5,000/month cleared the P2 Employment Pass qualifying salary in force in 2010 — S$3,500, raised to S$4,000 in December 2011. No labor market test applied to EP holders in 2010. Processing: days.

3. The tax wedge

 
France (€40,000 gross)
Singapore (S$60,000 gross)
Employee social charges
~22–25% (cadre)
0% — EP holders exempt from CPF
Income tax (single)
~€2,500–3,000
~S$2,500–3,500 (YA2011 brackets)

~€27,000–28,000
~S$56,500–57,500 (≈€31,400–31,900)
Retention

Capital gains
Taxed (~18% + social levies)
Not taxed
Note that France's ~30% wedge is not pure extraction: it funds pension, healthcare, and unemployment insurance. Singapore's ~5% means the safety net is self-built. The arbitrage is real, but it transfers risk to you.

4. Six-month liquidity

 
France (waiting)
Singapore (working)
Net income, 6 months
€0
~S$28,500 (≈€15,800)

Swing ≈ €15,000 over six months.
 
Method note: the foregone Paris salary is not an additional cost — the counterfactual Paris cash flow is zero; that is the premise.
 
Year 1 extension (assumption-dependent): if the French permit lands at month 6, the French path saves ~€1,700 for the year against Singapore's ~€18,300 — a ~€16,500 gap.

5. The real arbitrage is the savings rate

Singapore gross was lower in euro terms (€33,300 vs €40,000). Yet:
 
  • Singapore: ~€1,530/mo saved ≈ 55% of gross
  • Paris (once working): ~€1,290/mo saved ≈ 39% of gross
 
Note: EUR/SGD moved from ~2.00 (Jan 2010) to ~1.72 (Dec 2010) — roughly 14% euro depreciation. This is a euro-denominated valuation gain on SGD savings, not a rise in Singapore purchasing power. MAS's basket-band-crawl framework leaned toward appreciation post-2009. Untaxed gains on invested savings complete the effect.

6. Reversibility and positioning

Real option. Singapore was reversible: failure after 12–18 months still left the French master's, a Fortune 500 line on the CV, and hard-currency savings. The wait in France was not: six months of prime earning years, non-refundable, against a non-renewable permit.
 
Positioning. France: an oversupplied market of comparable graduates plus visa friction — a price-taker. Singapore: a talent-scarce regional hub, with APAC P&L exposure rather than a siloed domestic desk. Language was an operational ramp-up cost, not a structural barrier; twelve months of regional calls produced working trilingual capability (lived experience, not a statistic). Proximity: Saigon ~2h, Hanoi ~3.5h from Singapore; Paris–Vietnam ~12h.

7. Macro backdrop

Singapore 2010 real GDP growth ≈14.5–15% (MTI/SingStat). France ≈2% (INSEE), with the eurozone sovereign debt crisis unfolding. French unemployment did not peak in 2010 — it climbed to ≈10% by 2015 (INSEE, series-dependent). The exit was five years early, not late.

8. What would falsify this thesis

This is not a claim that Singapore beats France. It is a claim about 2010 conditions. The case collapses if: the French permit had been fast and near-certain; the Singapore role had no regional scope; the French welfare bundle were valued above ~25% of gross; the SGD had depreciated; or the operator could not function in English.

Sources (period-correct; identifiers + official archives)

  • INSEE — Enquête Emploi, BIT unemployment, France métropolitaine, 2008–2015; Tableaux de l'économie française 2010/2011 → insee.fr
  • CESEDA art. L.311-11, version in force 2009–2010; loi n° 2006-911 du 24 juillet 2006 → legifrance.gouv.fr ("version en vigueur à la date")
  • Code du travail, L.5221-2 and R.5221-* (2009–2010)
  • SMIC decrees, JORF July 2009 (€8.82/h) and January 2010 (€8.86/h) → legifrance.gouv.fr / INSEE SMIC series
  • DG Trésor, Trésor-Éco n° 92 (2011), youth unemployment → tresor.economie.gouv.fr
  • IRAS — historical resident rates, YA2011 → iras.gov.sg

The point is not to romanticise migration. It is to stop romanticising sunk costs. Your time is capital. Spend it where odds, cash flow, and exit options improve — not where nostalgia feels safest. 

Life choices are money choices. Count them.
